This section examines Chapter 3 — Mutation
is a hypothesis

about locality (7–8 minutes) from first
principles. Keep two questions

separate: does changing the order change
the measured outcome, and

does the proposed search method beat a
matched alternative at

the same distinct-evaluation budget? Use
the same starting ordering for

all operators: Swap: exchange two
positions. Insert: remove one item

and reinsert it. Inversion: reverse a
contiguous segment. Scramble: randomly

shuffle a segment. Portfolio: choose an
operator uniformly per mutation

event. Adaptive: reweight operators using
recent improvements. For each

operator, show the exact before-and-after
ordering, then the structure it

changes efficiently: . Landscape structure
. Matched operator . Intuition

belongs in a slot . swap . directly
repairs two

locations . . item must precede another .
insert .

changes many before/after relations
efficiently . . neighboring pairs matter

. inversion . repairs routes and adjacency
while preserving segments

. Build the Cayley graph of S_3 node by
node.

Explain that a mutation operator defines
the graph’s edges, so

“nearby” is operator-dependent. State the
mature lesson: choosing a mutation

is choosing a representation of local
structure. The distinction is

part of the result. A large ordering
effect does not

automatically imply an evolutionary-search
advantage, and almost-sure

convergence does not promise practical
efficiency.
